strengths: The paper addresses a genuine theoretical gap: despite prior work on SE(3) synchronization with dual quaternion representations (e.g., Hadi et al., 2024), no finite-iteration recovery guarantees existed for this formulation. The paper identifies and explicitly tackles the substantive technical obstacles unique to dual quaternions (ring with zero divisors, dual-number seminorm modulus not controlling components, lexicographic order vs. Euclidean error metrics).

The theoretical development is complete and self-contained: full proofs are provided in the appendix, including a careful Lipschitz analysis of the normalization/projection map (Lemma 2.5), a closed-form projection onto UDQ^n (Proposition 2.7), and an error-bound condition (Lemma D.5) that is actually tighter than the analogous SO(d) result in Liu et al. (2023). The separation of standard-part and dual-part error analysis (Remark 3.1) is thoughtful.

The experimental evaluation is reasonably broad: synthetic benchmarks under additive and Gaussian-mixture heavy-tail noise, partial observation via ER graphs, four Stanford object datasets, and 3DMatch scenes, with runtime comparisons and an observed linear error contraction consistent with Theorem 3.2.

The conceptual framing (Table 1, the 'eigenspace–sync gap' between relaxed eigenspace geometry and gauge symmetry) is a useful lens for understanding why matrix-based rounding heuristics are unstable, and motivates the dual quaternion formulation.
weaknesses: The algorithmic contribution is modest: spectral initialization followed by projected power iteration is a direct adaptation of the well-established GPM template (Boumal 2016; Liu et al. 2017, 2023; Ling 2022) to the dual quaternion algebra. The novelty rests mainly on the analysis, and the paper would benefit from a sharper articulation of what is fundamentally new versus transferred.

The central refinement guarantee (Theorem 3.2) rests on three auxiliary assumptions (7)-(9) — bounded aligned translations B, uniform nondegeneracy of projection inputs, and a gauge-switching condition with constant γ — whose validity for the actual iterates is not established or empirically verified. Condition (9) in particular assumes a bound on the very quantity the theorem is trying to control, which weakens the strength of the claimed recovery guarantee.

The noise regime ∥∆∥op ≤ n/350 is restrictive (a constant times n in operator norm), and the claimed advantage of DQGPM over the rounded spectral estimator (Remark 3.3) only materializes under an additional alignment condition on ∆x̂; the practical significance of this comparison is limited.

Experimental evidence has gaps: SDR is excluded from the sparse synthetic setting, the improvement over EIG in the dense regime (p = 0.30) is modest (e.g., 0.027 vs 0.032 rotation error), and on 3DMatch the baseline errors (1.3-2.0 rad) indicate the baselines essentially fail while DQGPM achieves near-exact recovery (errors of order 1e-5 to 1e-7) — such extreme separation when using gt.log measurements as input, evaluated on observed edges, raises questions about the evaluation protocol and whether the comparison is informative.

The conceptual 'eigenspace-sync gap' argument for the dual quaternion representation's superiority (Section 1, Table 1) is informal; no theory quantifies that the dual quaternion relaxation is fundamentally better than matrix spectral relaxations beyond the empirical results.

Presentation issues: the code availability sentence is incomplete ('available at' with no URL, Section 4), the concurrent citation 'Zhao et al. (2026)' is cited with future venue details, and the Impact Statement is a boilerplate placeholder.

strengths: Genuinely nontrivial technical hurdles are identified and addressed: dual quaternions form a ring with zero divisors, the modulus is only a seminorm, and eigenvalue ordering is lexicographic rather than Euclidean. The proofs (Lipschitz property of the normalization map, closed-form projection onto UDQ^n, error-bound condition in Lemma D.5) are carried out carefully and in detail.

The conceptual framing of the 'eigenspace–synchronization gap' (Table 1) is a nice organizing idea that explains why rounding is easy for SO(2)/SO(d) but heuristic for matrix-based SE(3) representations.

The claimed result (first finite-iteration recovery guarantees for SE(3) synchronization in the dual quaternion formulation) is a meaningful gap to fill, and the two-stage spectral + GPM design follows a well-tested template from phase/rotation synchronization.

Experiments cover both synthetic settings (varying noise, sparsity, heavy-tailed outliers, scalability) and real data (Stanford models, 3DMatch), with reasonable baselines (EIG, SPEC, SDR) and runtime comparisons.
weaknesses: Novelty relative to the closest prior work is under-argued. Hadi et al. (2024) already perform SE(3) synchronization via eigenvectors of dual quaternion matrices — essentially the same representation and a spectral estimator — yet the paper uses that work only for the evaluation metric and does not compare against it experimentally or clearly delineate what is new beyond adding a GPM refinement and error bounds. This is the most natural baseline and its omission is a significant weakness.

The central 'recovery guarantees' rest on conditions that are difficult or impossible to verify a priori: bounded aligned translations (7), a uniform nondegeneracy condition on projection inputs (8), and a gauge-switching leakage constant γ (9). These are assumptions on the unknown ground truth and iterate trajectory, weakening the practical force of Theorem 3.2 compared to the clean operator-norm assumptions in the SO(d) literature it builds on.

There is a theory–practice mismatch in the noise model. The analysis assumes additive, operator-norm-bounded Hermitian noise ∆ on the measurement matrix, whereas the experimental pipeline perturbs relative poses on the group (and real measurements come from ICP). The paper does not bridge these two noise regimes, and the theoretical threshold ∥∆∥op,st ≤ n/350 does not translate to the experimental settings (e.g., p = 0.05 with 95% missing edges), where the guarantees do not apply.

The synthetic noise model itself is artificial: ∆ is built from i.i.d. unit dual quaternions (Ξ − 1_{n×n}), which produces measurement matrices quite unlike those arising from perturbed relative poses. Results under this model may overstate the advantage over matrix-based baselines, several of which fail catastrophically in Table 2 (SPEC error ~1.6–2.0 rad), raising questions about baseline tuning.

Inconsistencies in experimental reporting: the caption of Table 2 excludes SDR 'due to limited scalability under uniform edge dropout,' yet SDR runs fine on the real datasets in Tables 4 and 6 (all with n ≤ 60); the synthetic experiments also use only n = 100, so the scalability claim for SDR exclusion is not substantiated. The code availability statement is truncated ('available at' with no link), harming reproducibility.

Much of the analysis is a close adaptation of existing GPM machinery (Journee et al. 2010; Liu et al. 2017, 2023; Ling 2022); e.g., Lemmas D.2–D.3 are explicitly described as analogues of Liu et al. (2023). The conceptual contribution is a transfer of known techniques to a new algebra, which is useful but incremental.

The paper lacks a limitations section; the strong assumptions of Theorem 3.2, the adversarial sensitivity of the lexicographic alignment, and the theory–experiment gap are not candidly discussed. The impact statement is boilerplate.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important problem (SE(3) synchronization) and provides what appears to be the first finite-iteration recovery guarantee for synchronization over unit dual quaternions, closing a gap relative to prior guarantees for phase, rotation, and O(d) synchronization (Liu et al. 2017, 2023; Ling 2022).

The technical development is careful and self-contained: a closed-form metric projection onto UDQ^n (Prop. 2.7), a Lipschitz-type stability property of normalization (Lemma 2.5 with a complete proof), an equivalent QPQC formulation (Prop. 2.1), and error bounds for both the raw spectral estimator (Prop. 2.4) and the rounded estimator (Thm 2.8).

The DQGPM refinement with elementwise projection is an elegant way to enforce feasibility at every iterate, and the analysis establishes linear contraction up to an explicit noise floor (Thm 3.2) plus a finite-iteration corollary chaining spectral initialization with refinement (Cor. 3.4).

Experiments cover synthetic data (varying noise, sparsity, heavy-tailed outliers, problem scale) and real data (Stanford objects, 3DMatch), showing consistent accuracy improvements and substantial runtime savings over SDR and SPEC; code availability supports reproducibility.

The discussion of the eigenspace-synchronization gap (Table 1) gives useful conceptual motivation for why dual quaternions are a natural representation for rounding in SE(3) compared with matrix embeddings.
weaknesses: The headline 'recovery guarantees' rest on assumptions that are difficult to verify a priori: Theorem 3.2 requires (7) a bound B on aligned translations of the ground truth, (8) a nondegeneracy condition involving the iterates Cr^k relative to an unknown aligner z_k, and (9) a stable gauge-switching condition with an unspecified constant γ. These are iterate- and ground-truth-dependent, so the theorem is more of a conditional analysis than an end-to-end guarantee comparable to, e.g., spectral-estimator results where only noise size enters.

The noise requirement ‖Δ‖_op,st ≤ n/350 is quite restrictive, and the claimed advantage of DQGPM over the rounded spectral estimator hinges on ‖Δ‖_{2,st} ≤ c√n‖Δ‖_op,st with c < 2/3; the paper concedes only c = 1 holds automatically and that c ≈ 1/2 is 'typically' observed — this distributional claim is asserted rather than proved.

The additive dual-quaternion noise model C = x̂x̂* + Ξ is nonstandard: relative motions in practice come from ICP or pose-graph edges whose errors live in SE(3) tangent spaces, not as additive unit-dual-quaternion perturbations. The paper's justification of the shifted model (subtracting 1_n×n) is heuristic; the mapping between this model and realistic measurement noise is not rigorously established.

The least-squares objective is not outlier-robust; robustness under Gaussian-mixture corruption is shown empirically in Appendix F, but the paper itself notes gross outliers would require an additional robust layer, which is not developed or analyzed.

Novelty is incremental relative to closely related recent work: the dual-quaternion eigenvector approach to SE(3) synchronization already exists (Hadi et al. 2024, whose evaluation protocol the paper adopts), Cui & Qi (2024) provide the power method, and concurrent work (Zhao et al. 2026) studies matrix-based anchored spectral estimators for rigid-motion synchronization. The main new elements are the projection analysis and the contraction theorem, which are meaningful but specialized.

In some real-data settings (e.g., dense Stanford datasets, translation errors in Table 4) the baselines match DQGPM within reported precision, and synthetic gains shrink in the dense regime, so the practical advantage is clearest mainly in sparse regimes.

Presentation of the main theorem could be improved: Theorem 3.2's bound (10) involves many unexplained constants (186B, 7000/477n, 1050, etc.) that obscure interpretability, and the interplay between lexicographic dual-number order and the Euclidean distance metrics d_st/d_T (Remark 3.1) requires careful reading.
